newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia tense as campaign enters last leg.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia tense as campaign enters last leg.

text.p: Indonesia was calm on Monday after bouts of pre-election violence over the weekend, but police said they were on alert for fresh clashes when large-scale campaigning resumes on Tuesday.

"From the view of the national police, it's safe and under control (now)," national police spokesman Brigadier-General Nurfaizi told Reuters, adding security would remain place for the last few days of the campaign, which ends on Friday.
"The police are facing crowds which spontaneously arise in large numbers. If we act harshly, we will receive a response which will cause police or the community to suffer," he said.

Thousands of supporters of the minority Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) hurled stones at partisans of the ruling Golkar party and fought security forces in Jakarta and other major cities on Java island on Sunday, but there were no reports of serious injuries or arrests.

Police fired tear gas and rubber bullets and then fired in the air to disperse rioting mobs in Jakarta and charged protesters in the ancient city of Yogyakarta and the nearby town of Bantul, witnesses and newspapers said.
On Saturday, police fired into the air to disperse an angry mob of PPP supporters who said they were blocked from entering a street in eastern Jakarta where Golkar had campaigned earlier.

Though Monday was calm, police said trouble could flare again when the PPP resumes campaigning for the May 29 general elections on Tuesday on Java, home to 120 million of Indonesia's 200 million people and the site of most of the major pre-poll violence so far.
The three parties contesting the elections have agreed to campaign in different parts of the Moslem-majority country each day.
The third party in the contest, the ruptured Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), has drawn few crowds to its rallies and its campaigning on Java on Monday passed without incident.

The three political parties have said they will not hold any street rallies in Jakarta for the rest of the campaign because of the violence, but observers said it remained to be seen whether their supporters would obey orders.

Political analysts said Golkar, in power for the past 30 years under President Suharto's rule, was unlikely to be seriously challenged in the election, but they added that the current campaign was more heated than any previous one.

On Sunday, Suharto's eldest daughter Siti Hardianti Rukmana said her father was in good health, indicating he would probably run for a seventh five-year term when presidential elections are held next year.
"Thank God, he is still healthy," Rukmana, a senior Golkar official told Reuters while campaigning in central Java on Sunday.
The shrewd and sometimes ruthless former army general has ruled the world's fourth-most populous nation for over three decades with a firm hand, helped by a politicised military.
Concerns over his health periodically jolt the country as he has not publicly annointed a successor.
Separately, Golkar chief and Information Minister Harmoko said his party would not accept any limits on the presidency, another indication that Suharto, 75, was set for another term.
Political analysts have said the dissent shown during the campaign was mostly the expression of frustration by urban youth, and added it was only a short-term phenomenen.
Financial market analysts agreed, although they noted that trading in the rupiah and on the stock market was cautious on Monday in the wake of the weekend violence.
Jakarta stocks closed down 0.69 percent at 652.55 points, but dealers and brokers said price movements were within acceptable limits.
The rupiah was down to 2,442.50/3.50 against the dollar at the Jakarta close after opening at 2,438.0/40.0, but traders said the currency was stable.

"We see (election unrest) very much as a very, very short term impact, and really as of next Friday (when the campaign ends), all bets are on again," said Stephen Doe, director of research with Asia Equities Jasereh brokerage.
